claims.claim: The 1580 title page of the Ecclesiastical History names no author
The History was long credited to Beza; Reuss asks whether he wrote it and finds the tradition's foundations anything but solid
Reuss thought Beza did not compile the History himself but directed it closely and contributed his memories of the Colloquy of Poissy
Baum and Cunitz show the History's Poissy chapter copying La Place's Commentaires word for word in places
The History is a Reformed narrative, polemical in places, e.g. calling most prelates incapable of treating religion
Baum and Cunitz say Beza's speech of 9 September was probably first printed under his own care a few days after the colloquy
On 9 September, about noon, the court gathered in the great refectory of the nuns at Poissy
The king sat with Orleans and Navarre on his right, and the queen mother and the Queen of Navarre on his left
Three cardinals sat on each side of the hall, and below them thirty-six bishops and archbishops, with clergy and doctors behind
Sarpi gives six cardinals on 9 September. The OCR reads 'second of September'; the passage describes the session of 9 September
Pallavicino gives five cardinals besides the legate and forty bishops who had come for the Estates
The History says twelve ministers came with 22 deputies of the provincial churches, brought in by the Duke of Guise
Sarpi says the Protestant ministers were fourteen
The ministers stood bare-headed at the barrier, and Beza, chosen by the others, spoke
Beza wished that all might with one voice sing a hymn to the Lord and hold out hands to one another
Beza's printed speech: Christ's body is as far from the bread and wine as the highest heaven from the earth
The History's narrative: Christ's body, though truly offered and given in the Supper, was as far from the bread as heaven from earth
The prelates began to murmur; some said 'Blasphemavit', others rose to leave
Tournon asked the king and queen that Beza be silenced or allowed to withdraw
The History: the king did not stir, and Beza finished his speech
Sarpi: Beza spoke with such heat that he was commanded to conclude
Languet, in a note by Baum and Cunitz, says they let Beza finish
Catherine, on 14 September, says she nearly silenced Beza but held back; known through a note by Baum and Cunitz from Le Laboureur
Beza gave the confession of the Reformed churches to the king
Sarpi says Beza spoke after praying on his knee

After the first session the prelates resolved that Lorraine, helped by Despence, would answer on the Church and the Supper only. A counter-confession would follow, with condemnation for refusal. The History gives no date; dated 10 September by Baum and Cunitz from Vermigli's letter (HE1 l.29024-29027)
The second session was on 16 September in the same hall
Lorraine told the king he was the Church's son, not its lord; a member, not its head
The prelates' assembly received the Society of Jesus on Monday 15 September as a college, not a new order, on condition it take another title
The royal letters of 1562 call the Poissy meeting the 'assemblée du clergé et concile national'
The legate, Cardinal of Ferrara, came to court on 19 September, by Vermigli's Relatio in a note by Baum and Cunitz
The History says Lainez (called 'Lieva') was in the legate's train; the editors correct the name
Lainez's editors date his arrival at Paris on 17 September and at Saint-Germain on 19 September
On 24 September the History gives five cardinals, fifteen or sixteen doctors, some bishops, and twelve ministers only
Polanco dates the third meeting to Wednesday 24 September; his editors' note reads 24 September 1561
Polanco says on Friday 26 September the same five cardinals came, with 25 bishops, and the queen mother despite the rain
Polanco says Ferrara and Tournon would not attend these disputations
Martyr spoke in Italian on 26 September, at the queen's wish, Polanco says
Lainez spoke in Italian, always turning his speech to the queen, for about three quarters of an hour, Polanco says
Lainez: it is not for the queen, nor for temporal princes, to handle matters of faith; they belong to the pope and the general council
Lainez: with the general council open, such meetings were neither fitting nor lawful
Lainez's copy was begun by Codreto and finished by Polanco, with Lainez's own corrections, the editors say
Coudret says Polanco was present
Polanco's letter is printed from his own drafts, the editors say
The ministers' declaration of 26 September says they speak for a million people in France, Switzerland, Poland, Germany, England and Scotland
Lorraine produced a paper that proved a copy of a Württemberg preachers' confession of 1559
The History says Lorraine sent for Augsburg-confession ministers 'afin de les divifer'
The History says the third conference, the last, went without order or secretaries
At Catherine's order two bishops (Montluc, Du Val) and three doctors (Despence, Salignac, Boutelier) conferred with five ministers (Martyr, Beza, Des Gallars, Marlorat, L'Espine)
The conference met on 29 September; Baum and Cunitz correct the text's date
On 1 October the statement was recast at Despence's urging
The statement says Christ in the Supper truly gives the substance of his body and blood
The History says Lorraine said he had never believed otherwise; Des Gallars agrees, Beza's letter of 4 October is silent
The formula went to Poissy on 4 October and was rejected as captious on 9 October
The prelates' conclusion found the statement not only insufficient but captious, with errors
Unless Beza and his company at once confessed and signed the Catholic confession, they would not be heard again
The conclusion asks that they be barred from the realm under the king's penalty. There had been but one God, one king, one faith and one law
The Catholic confession says Christ's body and blood are present really and transubstantially under the species of bread and wine
The canons' preamble: the king summoned the prelates of the Gallican Church to Poissy, pending the general council
The canons submit all decrees to the pope
The first canon treats the naming and examination of bishops
The last canon tells the faithful to abhor Luther, Zwingli and Calvin as heresiarchs
The canons close 'Acta Poissiaci ... 1561. Pridie Idus Oct.', in Languet's Latin given by Baum and Cunitz
After 9 October the ministers could never obtain a debate on their confession, the History says
The prelates dismissed their doctors on 13 October and went home
The German theologians reached Paris on 19 October, Baum and Cunitz say
Catherine: the two meetings brought only confusion of disputes upon disputes, more discord than union

After Lorraine's reply, Catherine thought it good that the prelates enter a gracious colloquy with the ministers on their confession (the two meetings fit the sessions of 24 and 26 September, which Polanco dates)
Catherine's smaller conference of five or six did not please the other prelates
Catherine: nothing in the canons can remedy the troubles
Catherine will await the next general council, not knowing what to expect of it
Catherine's letter is dated at Saint-Germain, October 1561, signed CATERINE; the OCR of the day reads 'iS.'
The heading above Catherine's letter is Aymon's
Sarpi: the Pope was very glad the colloquy was dissolved without doing anything
Pallavicino: neither side surrendered, and each claimed a kind of victory
Pallavicino: French Catholics blamed the colloquy for the Huguenots' freedom to profess their faith openly
Pallavicino: no national council was agreed. Catholics thought it an insult to the general council; the Reformed knew French prelates would not grant them equal judging power
Bonnet: the colloquy everywhere increased the audacity of the Reformed
The Edict of January suspended penalties for Reformed meetings by day outside the towns. It did so until the general council decided or the king ordered otherwise
The Edict's reason: awaiting God's grace to reunite the subjects in one fold
The Edict also forbids preaching inside the towns, by day or night
Waterworth: the articles proposed at Poissy were secretly submitted to canonists at Trent in 1562, to be examined
Pallavicino reports Lorraine at Trent, 1563: the clergy and Estates gathered at Poissy were held back with great difficulty
A 1607 letter the diary's editor gives to James Melvill (the attribution in square brackets) cites the Colloquy of Poissy as a warning against colloquies
Melville's letter is in the 1607 continuation of his diary
Bersier: in 1872 the synod president opened a session with Beza's confession of sins first read at Poissy
The July assembly resolved again to call the prelates to Poissy. The ministers would have safe-conduct to be heard, to see whether they could be reunited to the Roman Church
Baum and Cunitz say that assembly's deliberations ran from 23 June to 11 July
The History says the assembly made the Edict of July
Bretagne, speaking for the Third Estate, asked the king to call a free and lawful national council and preside over it
A further list of requests at the Estates asks for a free and lawful national council, as already promised
L'Hospital, in the History's summary: the king granted a safe-conduct hoping a friendly conference would profit, so no one could say they were condemned unheard
The ministers asked that bishops not be their judges, being the other party, and that all be decided by the word of God alone
The king: 'je vous ay fait affembler'
Martyr and Beza were sent for by letters of the King of Navarre; Martyr from Zurich, Beza from Geneva
Des Gallars had been pastor of the London church for two years, the editors say
The History names fourteen ministers in all
Baum and Cunitz count La Tour as the twelfth minister and the lay deputies as 22
Polanco names the five cardinals of 24 September as Lorraine, Armagnac, Bourbon, Chatillon and Guise
The queen gave the ministers her word that the clergy would not be their judges, with the Admiral present
The title of one early edition of Beza's speech, listed by Baum and Cunitz, calls 9 September a Tuesday
The ministers' first petition is dated 17 August in the History
Languet wrote on 1 August that the bishops' assembly had begun three days before. Brulart gives 1 August; De Thou 10 August, which the editors reject
Polanco's 26 September formula reads 'substantialiter'; the History prints a French statement without it
Pallavicino is of the Society of Jesus (title)
Lainez is called general of the Society of Jesus by Pallavicino
Calvin advised Beza by letter, 10 and 24 September 1561
Crespin's notice nearly reproduces La Place's narrative, Benoît says
Beza was minister at Geneva then
Beza's printed speech: believers are made partakers of Christ's body and blood in a spiritual way and through faith, as truly as they see the sacraments
Sarpi was a Venetian friar of the Servite order
Pallavicino's history sets out to refute a false history published under the name Pietro Soave Polano (Sarpi) (title)
Sarpi writes against the papal power: the council confirmed the 'exorbitant power' of the See of Rome

contested_claims.sides: Credited to Beza by long tradition and by the Library catalogue (beza_histoire-ecclesiastique-t1-fra_baum-cunitz1883.txt l.2); the 1580 title page names no author (beza_histoire-ecclesiastique-t1-fra_baum-cunitz1883.txt l.110-130) | Reuss: Beza directed it and gave his Poissy memories but did not compile it (beza_histoire-ecclesiastique-t3-fra_baum-cunitz-reuss1889.txt l.2002-2010) | Soldan and Heppe, cited by Reuss, deny Beza wrote it (beza_histoire-ecclesiastique-t3-fra_baum-cunitz-reuss1889.txt l.1629-1648)
contested_claims.note: The entry never calls the History Beza's; it prints his speech as participant words.

contested_claims.claim: Whether Beza was stopped on 9 September
contested_claims.sides: He was told to conclude: Sarpi (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.42836-42838) | The king did not stir and Beza finished: the History (beza_histoire-ecclesiastique-t1-fra_baum-cunitz1883.txt l.28722-28727); Languet, in a note (beza_histoire-ecclesiastique-t1-fra_baum-cunitz1883.txt l.28771-28773); Catherine of 14 September says she nearly silenced him but held back (beza_histoire-ecclesiastique-t1-fra_baum-cunitz1883.txt l.28785-28812) | Brulart, in a note, says he was interrupted and lost his thread (beza_histoire-ecclesiastique-t1-fra_baum-cunitz1883.txt l.28736-28741)

'du pain & du vin ... le plus haut ciel': the printed speech (beza_histoire-ecclesiastique-t1-fra_baum-cunitz1883.txt l.28515-28517) | 'du pain ... le haut des cieux', with the concessive 'combien qu'il nous fust véritablement offert & communiqué': the History's narrative (beza_histoire-ecclesiastique-t1-fra_baum-cunitz1883.txt l.28709-28713)

contested_claims.sides: He said he had never believed otherwise: the History (beza_histoire-ecclesiastique-t1-fra_baum-cunitz1883.txt l.33400-33405); Des Gallars, in a note (beza_histoire-ecclesiastique-t1-fra_baum-cunitz1883.txt l.33445-33449) | Beza's letter of 4 October says nothing of it, Baum and Cunitz note (beza_histoire-ecclesiastique-t1-fra_baum-cunitz1883.txt l.33444)
